title: Plain Urban Water Networks: Percolation Theory as a Tool for Bottleneck Identification and Connectivity Enhancement
content:
Abstract

Plain urban water networks generally exhibit weak hydrodynamic conditions and limited hydraulic connectivity, resulting in multiple challenges related to flooding, water quality, and aquatic ecosystems. A favorable spatiotemporal hydrodynamic regime is essential for water networks to enhance connectivity and maintain their functional performance. Quickly identifying hydrodynamically weak bottleneck segments can support targeted improvement of the hydrodynamic regime of water networks. However, traditional scenario enumeration and scheme comparison are time-consuming and provide limited guidance on which segments should be prioritized for improvement. This study presents a framework for identifying and prioritizing hydrodynamic bottleneck segments in water networks based on percolation theory. By integrating one-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation with graph models, functional states (functional/non-functional) are mapped into segments based on flow velocity thresholds, with segments below the thresholds classified as non-functional. Bottleneck segments that most strongly control velocity-based connectivity are then identified by tracking the critical transition threshold of the largest connected component. Improving the identified bottleneck segment enhanced network connectivity more than improving a segment with high betweenness centrality. As the bottleneck shifts to other segments once the original bottleneck is sufficiently improved, a cascading bottleneck prioritization method is proposed to update the bottleneck sequence and guide phased improvements. This approach provides a quantitative basis for progressively strengthening velocity-based network connectivity. Comparative hydrodynamic modeling experiments supported the hydraulic consistency of bottleneck identification and improvement, while increasing computational efficiency by 70.6 times. Experiments on random geometric graphs further showed that water networks with similar structural degree patterns can exhibit comparable percolation behavior.
